strengths: The paper systematically explores replacing Transformer blocks in HuBERT with Mamba blocks, covering pretraining, fine-tuning, representation analysis, and probing across multiple settings, which is a useful and timely empirical contribution for speech SSL.

Computational efficiency claims are supported with MACs and RTF measurements across sequence lengths, clearly showing near-constant cost for Mamba versus quadratic growth and OOM for Transformer models on long sequences.

Long-context ASR experiments on TEDLIUM3 provide direct evidence that bidirectional Mamba-based HuBERT can process document-level inputs and improve WER, whereas the Transformer baseline fails due to memory limits.
Causal/streaming ASR results show a Mamba-based model with fewer parameters outperforming a larger Causal Transformer, supporting the practical value of Mamba for low-latency speech recognition.

The representation analyses, including layer-wise phone purity and CCA with phone, speaker, and emotion embeddings, plus ablations over ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba, add useful qualitative insight beyond aggregate WER numbers.
The comparison trains Transformer baselines from scratch under the same pipeline, and the long-context WER improvement is supported by a paired t-test, which strengthens internal validity.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the main contribution is replacing Transformer blocks with existing Mamba blocks in HuBERT, and prior Mamba-based speech SSL work already exists, so the claim of being the first comprehensive exploration may be overstated.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code, checkpoints, or full hyperparameter details are provided, and the single-GPU training setup with altered batch size and iteration count differs substantially from standard HuBERT training, making exact reproduction difficult.

The evaluation is not comprehensive enough for strong general claims: SUPERB probing uses only four MiniSUPERB tasks, no direct spoken language modeling with quantized units is performed, and ASR is limited to TEDLIUM3 plus one streaming setup.

Some conclusions rely on proxy metrics and descriptive trends: phone purity and CCA similarities are not validated by downstream tasks such as speaker verification or spoken LM, and most results lack error bars or statistical significance tests.

Bidirectional scalability is inconsistent: ExtBiMamba underperforms the Transformer at base size across most SUPERB metrics, so the scalability claim is qualified and architecture-dependent, with only two bidirectional Mamba variants tested.

Compute comparisons are not always parameter-controlled: the causal Mamba model has 78.2M parameters versus 94.7M for the Causal Transformer, and MACs/RTF comparisons may be confounded by different model sizes, even if this often favors Mamba.

The long-context advantage is partly demonstrated through Transformer OOM failure, but no memory-efficient attention baselines (e.g., FlashAttention, chunked attention, or long-context Transformer variants) are compared, making the long-context claim less conclusive.
Generalization is not established beyond English TED talks, and the paper does not test whether the observed representation benefits transfer to other languages, domains, or speech SSL frameworks.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study of Mamba-based HuBERT for speech SSL, covering pretraining, causal/bidirectional ASR fine-tuning, long-context and streaming ASR, representation analysis, and SUPERB probing.
Clear computational efficiency analysis: MACs and RTF measurements across sequence lengths show linear scaling for Mamba and quadratic/out-of-memory behavior for Transformer baselines.
Practical long-context ASR advantage: document-level fine-tuning reduces WER from 13.37% to 11.08% while Transformer baselines fail due to OOM errors.
Causal ASR result shows parameter efficiency: 78.2M Mamba Base achieves 15.77% WER, outperforming a 94.7M causal Transformer (16.66% WER).
Representation analysis via phone purity and CCA provides useful insight into phonetic and speaker-related feature encoding, with Mamba showing distinct layer-wise behavior.
Ablation of ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba across base and small scales offers practical design guidance for bidirectional Mamba SSL architectures.
Honest reporting of mixed results, including bidirectional scalability challenges, which strengthens the credibility of the empirical findings.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the work primarily replaces Transformer blocks with Mamba blocks in HuBERT and provides an empirical benchmark, without introducing a new training objective or architecture. Prior Mamba-based speech SSL work exists, so the 'first comprehensive exploration' claim may be overstated.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or model release is mentioned, exact hyperparameters are incomplete, and training is conducted on a single GPU with altered batch size and reduced total audio duration, which may limit generalizability of the comparisons.
Evaluation is limited to MiniSUPERB subset and TEDLIUM3; full SUPERB, other SSL frameworks (e.g., wav2vec 2.0), and memory-efficient Transformer baselines for long-context ASR are not compared.

Some claims are only partially supported: causal Mamba does not outperform on all SUPERB tasks (e.g., IC and ER), bidirectional base ExtBiMamba underperforms Transformer across all metrics, and CCA speaker-feature advantages do not consistently translate to downstream gains.
Figure 1's RTF plot is confusing: the y-axis ranges from 0 to 1800 and appears to contradict the text claim that Mamba maintains lower RTF values, reducing clarity around a central efficiency claim.
Statistical significance testing is only reported for long-context ASR; SUPERB probing and representation analyses lack confidence intervals or significance tests.

Comparison fairness is uneven: Mamba Base has fewer parameters than Transformer Base, and Mamba+MLP is not consistently the best variant. The long-context ASR advantage relies heavily on the Transformer's OOM failure rather than WER superiority at utterance level.
Training from scratch under constrained compute makes it unclear how the findings would translate to standard large-scale SSL pretraining, limiting practical impact and broader applicability.

strengths: Broad, multi-faceted empirical study: the paper covers fine-tuning (long-context ASR on TEDLIUM3, causal/streaming ASR), downstream probing (four SUPERB tasks), and representation analyses (phone purity of quantized units, CCA with phoneme/speaker/emotion labels), giving a reasonably complete picture of Mamba-based HuBERT behavior rather than a single-task evaluation.

The efficiency characterization (MACs/G per second and RTF vs. sequence length) is clearly presented and usefully quantifies the linear vs. quadratic scaling, including the practical OOM threshold (~80s) for the causal Transformer under naive attention.

Reporting is mostly honest: the paper explicitly acknowledges mixed results, e.g., the bidirectional scalability limitation of ExtBiMamba and the ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba discrepancy, rather than hiding them.

Some concrete, potentially actionable findings for the speech SSL community: higher phone purity of Mamba's quantized representations in the causal setting, and a lower streaming ASR WER (15.77% vs. 16.66%) at a smaller parameter count.
The paper is generally well-organized and readable, with a clear motivation and a logical experimental progression.
weaknesses: The headline long-context claim is confounded. Table I compares document-level ExtBiMamba (11.08% WER) against utterance-level Transformer (11.86%) only because the dense Transformer OOMs; no memory-efficient Transformer baseline (chunked/streaming attention, gradient checkpointing, FlashAttention) is attempted. The reported gain may therefore stem from using document context rather than from the Mamba architecture, so the central 'Mamba enables long-context ASR' claim is not established.

Parameter-matched comparisons are missing. The streaming claim contrasts a 78.2M Mamba against a 94.7M causal Transformer; to substantiate the 'better accuracy with fewer parameters' claim, a 78.2M causal Transformer (or a 94.7M Mamba) baseline is required and is absent.

Models are trained at a heavily reduced scale (single GPU, per-batch audio ~1/4 of the original HuBERT setup, 250k+400k steps) and are never compared to published HuBERT/SSL baselines. It is unclear whether the architecture comparisons transfer, and 'competitive performance' is only relative to the authors' own reduced-scale Transformer, not to wav2vec 2.0, WavLM, data2vec, or SOTA.

No variance or error bars. Results appear to be single runs with no seeds, yet several claims rest on ~1% WER or ~1 SUPERB-point margins (e.g., 15.77 vs. 16.66; 823.15 vs. 805.44), which may be within noise.

Novelty is limited. Prior work already applies Mamba/SSMs to speech and to speech SSL ([16], [17], [5]-[8]); the contribution is essentially an architecture swap plus evaluation, so the 'first comprehensive exploration' framing overstates the delta.

Reproducibility gaps: no optimizer/learning-rate/schedule details, no code or model release mentioned, and the inherited 'HuBERT pipeline' details only partially apply given the altered batch size and iteration count. Training stability is not discussed.

Results that undercut the general claims are not adequately reconciled: ExtBiMamba loses to the Transformer across all SUPERB tasks in the base bidirectional setting (815.38 vs. 868.93), and the paper acknowledges but does not investigate why higher phone purity does not translate into better probing.

The abstract and introduction overclaim relative to the evidence, e.g., 'superior performance when fine-tuned for streaming ASR' rests on a single non-parameter-matched comparison, and 'competitive performance on SUPERB' holds only in the causal setting.
The CCA and phone-purity analyses are computed only on the authors' own models with no reference to published representations, limiting their interpretive value.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely question: whether Mamba-based architectures can serve as effective alternatives to Transformers for speech self-supervised learning.
Includes a diverse empirical suite covering computational efficiency, ASR fine-tuning in causal/long-context settings, SUPERB probing, and layer-wise representational analyses.
Provides useful reproducibility details, including single-GPU training setup, hyperparameters, and architectural definitions for Mamba and bidirectional variants.

Reports some practically interesting observations, e.g., linear-time scaling enables document-level ASR where causal Transformer OOMs, and causal Mamba attains lower WER than a larger causal Transformer.
weaknesses: Experimental rigor is insufficient: all models are trained on a single GPU, with a batch size 1/4 of the original HuBERT, and results come from a single training run without multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests for most comparisons. Small reported gains may therefore be noise.

The scale of pre-training is far below standard SSL practice, making the central claims about Mamba-based speech SSL models' competitiveness and scalability weak; the observed bidirectional scaling difficulty is based on one small-scale training run rather than a systematic scaling study.

Novelty and contribution are overstated: swapping Transformer blocks for Mamba in HuBERT is a straightforward architectural substitution, and prior work has already explored Mamba for speech SSL; the 'first comprehensive exploration' claim is not well supported.

Key baselines and comparisons are missing or unfair: no comparison to official HuBERT under equivalent compute, no other efficient architectures (e.g., Conformer, alternative SSMs), and long-context ASR compares only against utterance-level Mamba without chunking or other long-form baselines.

Several conclusions are not adequately supported by the evidence: e.g., claims that Mamba captures speaker-related features more distinctly, or that higher phone purity benefits spoken language modeling, are inferential and not directly tested; mixed SUPERB results (Transformer dominates in bidirectional base) are downplayed.

Evaluation scope is narrow: SUPERB_S in the main tables is computed from only four tasks, and the paper omits downstream generative or spoken language modeling evaluations despite motivating them in the abstract and contributions.

Presentation and reproducibility have issues: the code link is incomplete in the abstract, some figures/tables are difficult to interpret without additional context, and training stability analyses are not clearly tied to downstream performance.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive empirical exploration of Mamba-based HuBERT models across causal, bidirectional, long-context, and streaming ASR settings, as well as SUPERB probing.

It clearly demonstrates computational advantages: MACs and RTF measurements show Mamba's near-constant cost with sequence length and its ability to process long audio where the Transformer baseline runs out of memory beyond 80 seconds.

The representation analyses are a useful contribution: layer-wise phone purity and CCA with phone, speaker, and emotion embeddings reveal that Mamba-based models can capture phonetic and speaker-related features distinctly and yield higher-quality quantized representations.

The ablation between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba, together with the training stability analysis, offers practical design guidance and identifies bidirectional scalability as a concrete challenge for future work.
The causal/streaming ASR results are promising: Mamba-based HuBERT achieves lower WER with fewer parameters than a causal Transformer (15.77% vs 16.66% at 78.2M vs 94.7M) and better causal SUPERB_S.

The paper is generally transparent about its setup: pretraining pipeline, hyperparameters, single-GPU constraints, and an appendix with full SUPERB evaluation and additional k-means phone-purity results.
The limitations section is honest about reduced training scale and the need for future scale exploration, which supports reproducibility and cautious interpretation.
weaknesses: The experimental scale is limited: models are trained on a single GPU with reduced batch size, only LibriSpeech 960h, and only Base/Small sizes. This constrains external validity, and conclusions about scalability may not hold at larger scales.

All results come from a single training run per configuration, with no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or variance estimates. Except for one paired t-test on long-context ASR, many model comparisons in Tables 3-5 may be within noise.

The attribution of ExtBiMamba Base underperformance to training instability is speculative. The loss-scale visualization is not a controlled intervention, and no alternative remedies or causal experiments are provided to establish this explanation.

The causal ASR comparison in Table 2 is not parameter-matched (Mamba 78.2M vs Causal Transformer 94.7M); the same-size Mamba+MLP variant is not reported for this task, leaving the strongest causal claim incomplete.

The long-context ASR experiment shows ExtBiMamba can process documents where the Transformer baseline OOMs, but it does not compare against a long-context Transformer with memory optimization, so superiority in long-context ASR is not fully established.

Some representation findings are not fully reconciled: Mamba variants show higher CCA similarity with speaker embeddings, but ExtBiMamba Base SID performance is worse than Transformer; similarly, higher phone purity does not always translate to better PR probing.

Novelty over prior Mamba speech SSL work is incremental: replacing Transformer blocks with Mamba blocks and evaluating HuBERT-style pretraining is a natural extension rather than a new method or training objective.
The codebase availability is indicated but no repository URL is visible in the provided manuscript, which weakens verifiability of reproducibility.
The paper does not discuss ethical or bias considerations for speech SSL models, such as robustness across accents or demographic groups.

strengths: Systematic and comprehensive empirical study of Mamba-based HuBERT for speech SSL, covering pretraining, long-context/causal ASR, SUPERB probing, and layer-wise representation analysis.

Clear computational efficiency analysis: Mamba-based HuBERT shows near-constant MACs and lower RTF for long sequences, while causal Transformer encounters OOM beyond 80 seconds, directly supporting long-context and streaming use cases.

Strong long-context ASR result: ExtBiMamba processes full documents and improves WER from 13.37% (utterance-level) to 11.08% (document-level), with a paired t-test reported (p=0.001); the Transformer baseline cannot run due to memory limits.

Competitive causal ASR and probing results: Mamba with 78.2M parameters outperforms a 94.7M causal Transformer on causal ASR WER (15.77 vs 16.66), and Mamba+MLP achieves the best causal SUPERB_S score (823.15).
Useful representation analyses: phone purity and CCA with speaker/emotion embeddings provide insight into why Mamba-based causal models perform well, even when the conclusions are nuanced.

Honest limitations section and reproducibility details: single-GPU training, hyperparameters, and reduced batch size are disclosed; the authors acknowledge that scale may affect conclusions and that bidirectional Mamba training is unstable.
Ablation of bidirectional Mamba variants (ExtBiMamba vs InnBiMamba) offers practical design guidance and identifies scale-dependent behavior, which is valuable for future work.
The paper is generally well written, with clear figures and tables, and is relevant to speech SSL, ASR, and spoken language modeling.
weaknesses: Limited training scale and single-run evaluation: models are trained on one V100 with roughly one-quarter of the original HuBERT batch size, with no multiple seeds or variance estimates, so the central comparisons may not hold at full scale.

Some claims are only partially supported: bidirectional Mamba (ExtBiMamba) underperforms Transformer at Base scale, phone purity does not consistently align with downstream fine-tuning gains, and the 'more distinct speaker-related features' claim is not uniformly true across settings.

Comparisons are narrow: only a Transformer trained from scratch under the same reduced setup is used as the main baseline; official HuBERT and other SSL models (wav2vec2, WavLM) or recent Mamba speech SSL methods are not directly compared.
Long-context ASR is evaluated only on TEDLIUM3, and causal ASR only on LibriSpeech 100h test-clean; broader datasets and streaming baselines (e.g., with lookahead) would strengthen the conclusions.
Most table comparisons lack statistical significance testing; only one paired t-test is reported, so small differences in SUPERB or WER may not be reliable.
Reproducibility is weakened by the unclear/missing codebase link and the absence of seed variance; bidirectional Mamba instability may make results sensitive to implementation and hardware.
Novelty is mostly empirical: Mamba has already been applied to speech and SSL, so the main contribution is a cross-task evaluation rather than a new method or theoretical insight.

Efficiency claims are based on MACs and RTF, but RTF for Mamba still increases with sequence length and may depend on kernel optimizations; algorithmic complexity does not fully guarantee wall-clock gains.
